segs.text: Inside the Strain. What happens inside a hamstring after a strain, from second zero to month six and beyond.
Most of this cellular timeline comes from rodent models. Human healing follows the same sequence, but probably runs more slowly, especially in larger injuries.
Skeletal muscle is built like a cable inside a cable inside a cable.
The epimysium, the deep fascia, wraps the whole muscle.
Perimysium wraps each bundle of fibers (fascicle). Endomysium wraps each individual fiber.
Between fascial layers, a hyaluronan-rich loose connective tissue, made in part by fasciacytes, lets the layers glide.
The basal lamina is fused to each fiber. Satellite cells, the muscle's stem cells, sit dormant just beneath it.
Each nucleus along the fiber manages one stretch of it: the myonuclear domain.
All layers are continuous with each other and the tendon, and pass force sideways: myofascial force transmission.
Strains usually happen during a forceful eccentric contraction, like the late swing phase of sprinting.
The hamstring is lengthening under load as the knee extends.
Failure usually occurs near the myotendinous junction or the aponeurosis.
The fibers rupture, and the broken ends recoil and retract, leaving a gap.
In shearing-type strains the basal lamina sleeves tear too, so regeneration is less orderly and more scar forms.
Capillaries in the gap tear and bleed.
Hematoma: blood fills the gap and clots into a fibrin mesh.
The fibrin net runs in every direction. It is a solid plug, not a hollow box.
Calcium pours into torn fibers through the ruptured membrane and stretch-activated channels.
Calcium activates calpain. With reactive oxygen species, damage spreads along the fiber: secondary injury.
Within hours, a contraction band of hypercontracted filaments reseals the membrane and stops the spread.
This happens automatically. It does not depend on the athlete contracting the muscle.
Torn vessels and swelling cut off oxygen to the area, which can kill more fibers.
Clinical tie-in. What limits secondary damage.
Stop activity right away. Compress and elevate to control bleeding and swelling.
Avoid eccentric loading in the first days.
Myth to correct: voluntary isometrics in the first hours do not "build" the contraction band. Tension across a fresh tear can widen the gap.
Immediate active mobilization in rats produced larger scars and frequent re-rupture. About 5 days of relative rest let granulation tissue bridge the gap first.
No proven treatment blocks the calcium cascade after injury in humans. Pre-exercise L-arginine shows promise as prevention only. Antioxidant supplements have not helped.
Damaged cells release alarm molecules (DAMPs) that call in immune cells.
Neutrophils arrive within hours.
Pro-inflammatory M1 macrophages follow and dominate the first ~3 days, engulfing necrotic debris.
Behind each contraction band the dead segment is cleared, leaving an empty basal-lamina tube.
TNF, IL-1β and IL-6 also tell satellite cells to wake up and multiply.
Inflammation here is not only damage. It is the starting signal for regeneration.
After eating dead cells (efferocytosis), macrophages reprogram into M2 "repair" macrophages.
M2 cells release IL-10, IGF-1 and growth factors that calm inflammation and drive satellite-cell differentiation and fusion.
M1 and M2 are ends of a continuum. Finishing the cleanup triggers the switch, not inflammation simply fading.
Repeated re-injury restarts M1 activity and pushes toward chronic inflammation and fibrosis.
NSAIDs block COX enzymes in the injured tissue, which lowers local prostaglandins.
Some of those prostaglandins are signals satellite cells use.
Acetaminophen works mainly in the central nervous system and has little effect on local prostaglandins.
In mice it did not impair regeneration.
Clinical tie-in. Pain medication during regeneration.
Short-term NSAID use gave small benefits in strength loss, soreness and CK. No human study followed outcomes beyond 14 days.
In animals, effects turned negative with longer courses or later timing. Ketorolac at 47 h impaired regeneration in mice, though the macrophage switch was unaffected.
Conflicting: ibuprofen 1,200 mg/day (2 wk before, 4 wk after) increased satellite-cell activation and sped remodeling at 30 days in an e-stim injury model.
Acetaminophen did not impair regeneration in mice.
Position: prefer acetaminophen for pain. If an NSAID is used, keep it short. Avoid regular use over several weeks during regeneration. Mind GI, kidney and bleeding risk.
New capillaries sprout from intact vessels at the edges and grow into the clot and granulation tissue.
They are visible by about day 3, driven by VEGF released by macrophages.
Oxygen delivery is rate-limiting. Regeneration moves only as fast as the supply lines advance.
The goal is to restore blood flow, not to flood the tissue with oxygen.
Shockwave in rats: one session increased satellite-cell recruitment, proliferation and differentiation.
Treated muscle reached at day 4 what untreated muscle reached at day 7. Controlled human trials in acute strains are lacking.
Clinical tie-in. Supporting the supply lines.
Support blood flow with pain-guided early movement, swelling control and nicotine avoidance.
Shockwave (ESWT): faster regeneration in rats. Reviews describe VEGF- and eNOS-driven vessel growth. Controlled human trials in acute strains are lacking.
Hyperbaric oxygen improved oxygenation and regeneration in rat contusions. Human data are lacking, and it is not standard care.
Fibrin and fibronectin from the clot cross-link into granulation tissue, a primary extracellular matrix.
It anchors fibroblasts, which lay down tenascin-C and fibronectin, then type III collagen.
New capillary loops make the tissue red and grainy, which is where "granulation" comes from.
Type III fibers start out disorganized. Type I, which provides most tensile strength, comes later.
The plug fills the gap stump to stump. In week one it holds, but tears easily.
Activated satellite cells switch on MyoD and Myf5 and multiply as myoblasts.
They multiply inside the empty basal-lamina tunnels.
They switch on myogenin and fuse into a multinucleated myotube.
Each nucleus can only support a limited length of fiber, so a long fiber needs many nuclei.
Some satellite cells self-renew, restocking the reserve for future injuries.
Myotubes become new fibers or fuse onto the surviving stumps.
Clinical tie-in. Electrical stimulation.
Rat strain model: low-frequency e-stim, 20 Hz, 30 minutes twice daily, started at day 5.
It increased MyoD and myogenin and produced more mature, well-ordered fibers.
Day 5 was chosen on purpose: after granulation tissue had bridged the gap.
From about day 5, regenerating stumps send out branches that pierce into both sides of the scar.
Each branch anchors to scar collagen through new mini-myotendinous junctions.
Day 14: the scar condenses, and the fibers close most of the gap.
Day 21: fibers from both sides interlace, with a thin seam of scar between them.
Nerves regrow along old paths and new NMJs form. Regeneration peaks ~2 weeks and slows by ~4 weeks.
Small gap with controlled scar: many fingers interlock.
Large gap with excessive scar: a dense wall blocks the fibers, which stop and curl.
Clinical tie-in. Tipping the balance toward muscle.
Keep the gap small with early compression and protection.
Relative rest for about the first 3–5 days, then progressive, pain-guided loading: isometric, then isotonic, then dynamic.
Avoid prolonged immobilization. It leads to a larger, more disorganized, contracted scar.
Too much TGF-β1 drives fibroblasts toward dense scar. Antifibrotic agents and PRP are experimental.
New fibers grow thicker, move their nuclei to the edge, and line up their sarcomeres. Capillaries are pruned back.
Collagen shifts from type III to type I, thickens, cross-links, and aligns with the direction of pull.
Fibroblasts become myofibroblasts, which pull on the collagen like tiny winches. The scar contracts.
Remodeling lasts months. In human strains, MRI still shows active repair at 6 months, after return to sport.
Loaded muscle: aligned collagen, thin scar.
Immobilized muscle: a tangled, shortened scar.
Clinical tie-in. Speeding the type III → type I shift.
Progressive mechanical loading drives collagen synthesis and alignment.
Ensure adequate protein and energy intake.
Avoid smoking and long courses of NSAIDs or corticosteroids.
Cross-linking runs on biological time. Loading improves quality and alignment more than it shortens the calendar.
Carla Stecco's group describes densification of the hyaluronan-rich layer between fascial sheets.
After trauma, overuse, disuse or inflammation, the layer becomes more viscous, without true fibrosis having to be present.
Gliding is reduced, and free nerve endings may become irritated.
Two depths: the collagen scar inside the muscle is permanent. Densified gel is proposed to be reversible.
Movement and manual shear are proposed to restore gliding. Direct human evidence for HA changes is limited.
The muscle model and the fascial model complement each other.
Clinical tie-in. Fascial work: evidence status.
Myofascial release is consistently associated with short-term improvements in pain and range of motion.
Long-term functional outcomes and direct structural change in fascia are inconsistent.
Best supported as an adjunct that helps athletes move and engage in active rehab, not as stand-alone treatment.
Proposed calcium–hyaluronan feedback loop; fascial stiffening may impair regeneration, so treat both muscle and fascia.
Timing: gentle work and movement around the injury in subacute and remodeling phases. No aggressive deep work on the tear in week 1.
The scar is not muscle. It is stiffer, does not contract, and changes how force passes through the muscle.
The folded myotendinous junction may never fully return. Atrophy and fat infiltration develop.
Neural inhibition: the injured muscle is under-activated, especially in eccentric work at long lengths.
Returning to sport before the tissue has matured contributes to the high re-injury rate.
Time the stimulus to the biology.
0–48 h: stop, compress, elevate, protect. No eccentric loading. Acetaminophen preferred.
Days 2–5: pain-free isometrics. Avoid both immobilization and aggressive loading.
Days 5–21: progressive isotonic, then dynamic loading. Gentle fascial work around the site.
Weeks 3–12: lengthening and eccentric work at long muscle lengths. Criteria-based return to sport.
Months 3–6+: keep up eccentric strengthening, like Nordic curls, after return to play.
Healing is a race between muscle regrowth and scar, inside a fascial system that has to keep gliding.
Protect the wet cement, feed the supply lines, load the rebuilders, align the rope, and keep the layers sliding.
